title: Profiling protein-protein interactions in human brain by refined co-fractionation mass spectrometry
projectDescription: Proteins are essential regulators of biological processes and can have diverse functions depending on their interactions with other proteins. To understand deeply the interaction and their complexes, co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS) was used with ion exchange chromatography columns and data was analyzed with Data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode. Our comprehensive DIA CF-MS analysis successfully identified over 1,000 protein complexes and approximately 10,000 protein-protein interactions, many of which had not been previously discovered. These findings present an invaluable resource for a wide range of human brain research endeavors, including the identification of disease-specific protein complexes.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Pooled human brain tissue samples were provided by Banner Sun Health Research Institute. 0.1 mg brain samples were lysed in 1mL of lysis buffer (10mM HEPES, 250 mM sucrose, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1% (v/v) dodecyl-b-D-maltopyranoside (DDM)) at the tissue: buffer ratio of 1:10 w/v. Freshly prepared 1 mM DTT, and 1X mM Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche) were added to the sample. Samples were homogenized using the Dounce homogenizer (45 beats). In the tissue lysate, 1.2uL of turbonuclease was added to hydrolyze any nucleic acids by incubating at 4℃ for 30 min. Sample lysate was centrifuged at 17K g for 30 minutes at 4℃ and protein supernatant was collected. Bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay and SDS-PAGE short gel were used to measure protein amount and concentration in the supernatant. Ion exchange chromatography columns made with weak anion-exchange PolyWAX LP column (200 x 2.1 mm i.d., 10 um, 1000-A; PolyLC Inc., MD, USA) was connected to two weak cation-exchange PolyCAT A (each 200 x 2.1 mm i.d., 10 um, 1000-A; PolyLC) for the protein complex separations. All buffers were made in fresh HPLC grade H2O. Buffer A comprised of no salt (10 mM HEPES and 3 mM NaN3, pH 7.6) and Buffer B contains high salt (Buffer A + 1.5 M NaCl). All HPLC fractionations were performed using an Agilent HPLC 1220 binary pump system (Agilent Technologies, ON, Canada). The columns were conditioned with buffer A before loading samples. In total, 500ug proteins was used for fractionation using the elution gradient consisting of 30 min flow of 100% buffer A. This was followed by 0-67% buffer B till 108 min and then 67-100% buffer B gradient from 108-130 min. The flow rate of HPLC was set at 0.1 ml/min. Protein elution was monitored by UV absorption at 280 nm. In total, 192 chromatography fractions were collected by collecting flow through in a new tube every 30 seconds. This process was repeated for both replicates. After the fractionation, each fraction was dried using SpeedVac concentrator. Each dried fractions (~2.5 ug total proteins) were dissolved in master mix consisting of 8M urea in 50mM HEPES, 5% Bovine serum albumin (BSA), 5mM DTT and Lys-C (pep:Lys-C = 1:100, w/w) using the Formulatrix Mantis automated liquid handling robot (Formulatrix). BSA (5% by volume) were spiked in each fraction for the internal normalization. Proteins were digested for 3 hours at RT. After digestion, urea concentration was reduced to 2M by diluting with 50mM HEPES buffer. Resulting sample mixture were again digested using trypsin (pep:tryp = 1:3, w/w) overnight. Peptides were reduced by addition of 1mM DTT for 30 min and alkylated with 3 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for another 30 min in the dark at RT. Finally, 10 mM DTT was added to quench the alkylation reaction and incubate another 30 min at RT. Digested peptide were aliquoted into two tubes and only one was utilized for further analysis. The peptides were desalted using standard method with slight change in washing step. To ensure the desalted peptides were free of salts, the washing step were repeated 15 times with 50uL wash buffer. Desalted peptides were dried using dried using SpeedVac concentrator. The dried peptides were resuspended in 10 μL of 5% formic acid and centrifuged at 21K g for 5 min. The resulting supernatant was then transferred into an HPLC insert tube and centrifuged again at 21K g for 10 min. For each fraction, 40% (or 4 μL) of the supernatant were injected into an RSLC nano system coupled with an Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). The peptides were separated using a 30 min gradient with a flow rate of ~0.25 μL/min and a column temperature of 65 ℃. The mass spectrometer was operated in data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode, with the following parameters: MS1 scan range of 400-1000 m/z, an isolation window of 20 m/z, window overlap of 1 m/z, default charge state of 2, MS1 and MS2 resolutions of 30K, 30% specified normalized collision energy for HCD fragmentation.
dataProcessingProtocol: The DIA data were analyzed using DIA-NN version 1.8.1 [24] with a spectral library consisting of 20,386 proteins generated from in silico tryptic digestion of the UniProt reviewed human database (March 2023). The spectral library was created through deep neural networks and included retention times for the mass range of 400-1000 m/z. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was selected as the fixed modification, while oxidation of methionine was set as the variable modification. For the data search, the raw files were searched against the in silico spectral library using the following parameters: missed cleavage of 2, carbamidomethylation as the fixed modification, oxidation as the variable modification, and a mass range of 400-1000 m/z. MBR was enabled for the data search, while all other parameters were kept at their default settings.
